nodes.title: torch.compile fullgraph=True is failing for GPTJ model for toy_backend

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug

The graph has a conv node in pytorch and a TensorRT node. The conv node has weight and bias lifted as placeholders. Hence we are seeing this runtime error of mismatch in the number of inputs.

Error message:
_check_input_constraints_for_graph(
  File "/root/.pyenv/versions/3.10.13/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/_export/utils.py", line 48, in _check_input_constraints_for_graph
    check(
  File "/root/.pyenv/versions/3.10.13/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/_export/utils.py", line 40, in check
    raise RuntimeError(msg)
RuntimeError: Unexpected number of inputs (expected 3, got 1)

If we unlift these parameters (i.e conv_weight and conv_bias are registered as get_attr nodes), there's a different error GraphModule does not contain attribute conv_weight
Reason:
This is because - syntax error occurs in _create_graph_module_for_export and hence the resulting gm does not have these attributes.

Steps to reproduce:
Install the nightly version of Torch-TRT
pip install --pre torch-tensorrt  --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu121

Run the following script to reproduce the error
import torch
import torch_tensorrt
import unittest

class MyModule(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 16, 3, stride=1, bias=True)
        self.relu = torch.nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        conv = self.conv(x)
        relu = self.relu(conv)
        mul = relu * 0.5
        return mul

input = torch.randn((1, 3, 224, 224), dtype=torch.float).to("cuda")
model = MyModule().eval().cuda()

compile_spec = {
        "inputs": [
            torch_tensorrt.Input(
                input.shape, dtype=torch.float, format=torch.contiguous_format
            )
        ],
        "ir": "dynamo",
        "min_block_size": 1,
        "torch_executed_ops": {"torch.ops.aten.convolution.default"},
    }

exp_program = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.trace(model, **compile_spec)
trt_gm = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.compile(exp_program, **compile_spec)
trt_exp_program = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.export(trt_gm, [input], ir="exported_program")

torch.export.save(trt_exp_program, "/tmp/trt.ep")
deser_trt_exp_program = torch.export.load("/tmp/trt.ep")
outputs_pyt = model(input)
outputs_trt = trt_exp_program(input)
Versions
[pip3] mypy==1.8.0
[pip3] mypy-extensions==1.0.0
[pip3] numpy==1.26.3
[pip3] pytorch-triton==2.2.0+e28a256d71
[pip3] torch==2.3.0.dev20240103+cu121
[pip3] torch-tensorrt==2.2.0.dev20240104+cu121
[pip3] torchvision==0.18.0.dev20240103+cu121

nodes.title: [export] Cannot perform inference if the ExportedProgram has weighted layers and custom ops

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
In PyTorch and Kineto, duration/timestamp are obtained(https://github.com/pytorch/kineto/blob/main/libkineto/src/CuptiActivity.h#L41, https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/csrc/autograd/profiler_kineto.cpp#L776) using microseconds. When converting from nanoseconds to microseconds, there can be a loss of precision. This can lead to significant loss in cases where a large number of events are captured. Is it possible to use nanoseconds? I think nanoseconds is better.
Versions
latest

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
I was using a SequentialLR to adjust my learning rate in the training process. However, a warning appeared:
UserWarning: The epoch parameter in `scheduler.step()` was not necessary
and is being deprecated where possible. Please use `scheduler.step()` to 
step the scheduler. During the deprecation, if epoch is different from None, 
the closed form is used instead of the new chainable form, where available. 
Please open an issue if you are unable to replicate your use case: 
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/new/choose.
warnings.warn(EPOCH_DEPRECATION_WARNING, UserWarning)

I checked my code and there was nothing like scheduler.step(epoch). After debugging, I found the problem was in torch\optim\lr_scheduler.py. The line scheduler.step(0) in SequentialLR.step caused the warning.
def step(self):
    self.last_epoch += 1
    idx = bisect_right(self._milestones, self.last_epoch)
    scheduler = self._schedulers[idx]
    if idx > 0 and self._milestones[idx - 1] == self.last_epoch:
        scheduler.step(0)
    else:
        scheduler.step()

    self._last_lr = scheduler.get_last_lr()

I wonder why there's a line scheduler.step(0) in SequentialLR. After all, the epoch parameter should be deprecated.

🐛 Describe the bug
Subindexing a matrix on the outer-dimensions before or after matrix multiplication should be the same: (A @ B)[:, U] === A @ B[:, U] because the results are independent. It is for CPU but not for MPS. Even for 2D matrices (so not even batched).
This makes PyTorch on MPS effectively useless. There is no point in using it if you cannot even assume that matrix multiplication is correct.
Example unit test:
import torch

def test_matmul_transpose_associativity(device):
    # Create a random matrix 16384x128
    x = torch.rand(16384, 128, device=device)
    # Create a random matrix 70000x128
    y = torch.rand(128, 70000,device=device)

    # Sample 23444 random indices from 70000
    indices = torch.randperm(70000, device=device)[:23444]

    # Select 23444 random rows from y
    y_sampled = y[:, indices]

    # Multiply x by y_sampled
    z_sampled = torch.matmul(x, y_sampled)
    # Multiply x by y
    z = torch.matmul(x, y)

    # z[:, indices] should be equal to z_sampled
    assert torch.allclose(z[:, indices], z_sampled, rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2), "Matmul associativity test failed on device {}".format(device)

test_matmul_transpose_associativity("cpu")
test_matmul_transpose_associativity("mps")
[42](file:///Users/akirsch/git/midjourney_explorations/spikes/matmul_mps?line=41) assert torch.allclose(z[:, indices], z_sampled, rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2), "Matmul associativity test failed on device {}".format(device)

🐛 Describe the bug
I am using the workflow described in PYTORCH 2.0 EXPORT POST TRAINING STATIC QUANTIZATION to quantize and export a model to my own backend.
I am noticing the following difference between capture_pre_autograd_graph and torch.export - capture_pre_autograd_graph doesn't capture descriptive node names from the original module source code while torch.export does capture this information. The following is a minimal example that illustrates this:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch._export import capture_pre_autograd_graph

# author a model.
class MLPNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(MLPNet, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(64, 64)
        self.relu1 = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(64, 32)
        self.relu2 = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(32, 16)
        self.relu3 = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc4 = nn.Linear(16, 8)
        self.relu4 = nn.ReLU()
        
    def forward(self, x):
        layer1 = self.relu1(self.fc1(x))
        layer2 = self.relu2(self.fc2(layer1))
        layer3 = self.relu3(self.fc3(layer2))
        y      = self.relu4(self.fc4(layer3))
        return y
    
    def name(self):
        return "MLP"

model = MLPNet().eval()

# generate a uniform distribution of data.
n_batches = 100
x_in = torch.distributions.uniform.Uniform(-1, 1).sample([n_batches, 64, 64])

# export the module (this will annotate the graph with node names such as
# "fc1_weight", "fc1_bias", ...)
m_export = torch.export.export(model, (x_in[0,:],))
print('---------------')
print('torch.export():')
print('---------------')
m_export.module().graph.print_tabular()
print()

# this won't do any annotations and going forward with quantization will lose
# node annotations.
m_pre = capture_pre_autograd_graph(model, (x_in[0,:],))
print('-----------------------------')
print('capture_pre_autograd_graph():')
print('-----------------------------')
m_pre.graph.print_tabular()
A snipped output is provided below:
---------------
torch.export():
---------------
opcode         name        target              args                     kwargs
-------------  ----------  ------------------  -----------------------  --------
get_attr       fc1_weight  fc1_weight          ()                       {}
get_attr       fc1_bias    fc1_bias            ()                       {}
get_attr       fc4_weight  fc4_weight          ()                       {}
[ ... ]
get_attr       fc4_bias    fc4_bias            ()                       {}
placeholder    arg8_1      arg8_1              ()                       {}
call_function  t           aten.t.default      (fc1_weight,)            {}
call_function  addmm       aten.addmm.default  (fc1_bias, arg8_1, t)    {}
call_function  relu        aten.relu.default   (addmm,)                 {}
call_function  t_1         aten.t.default      (fc2_weight,)            {}
[ ... ]

-----------------------------
capture_pre_autograd_graph():
-----------------------------
opcode         name              target               args                                          kwargs
-------------  ----------------  -------------------  --------------------------------------------  --------
placeholder    arg0_1            arg0                 ()                                            {}
get_attr       _param_constant0  _param_constant0     ()                                            {}
get_attr       _param_constant1  _param_constant1     ()                                            {}
call_function  linear            aten.linear.default  (arg0_1, _param_constant0, _param_constant1)  {}
call_function  relu              aten.relu.default    (linear,)                                     {}
get_attr       _param_constant2  _param_constant2     ()                                            {}
[ ...]

It would be desirable to preserve descriptive names such as "fc1_weight", "fc1_bias" etc., in the exported model which can be used further downstream to aid in debugging the model on a HW target. As such, the names in the graph are _param_constant0, _param_constant1 etc., which aren't very useful.
I have a couple of questions:

Is there a way to change this behavior in capture_pre_autograd_graph to match the information level captured via torch.export.export?
In torch.export.export would it be possible to capture the name the input variable (here, it is x) instead of arg8_1 (which cannot be traced back to x.

🐛 Describe the bug
The backward pass generated by TorchInductor does not follow expected behavior with channels_last memory format. The input to the backward pass (tangents_1 below) is not sent with channels_last format.
Here's the output_code.py call function for the backward pass
def call(args):
    primals_1, gt, tangents_1 = args
    args.clear()
    assert_size_stride(primals_1, (1, 320, 128, 128), (5242880, 1, 40960, 320))
    assert_size_stride(gt, (1, 320, 128, 128), (5242880, 1, 40960, 320))
    assert_size_stride(tangents_1, (1, 320, 128, 128), (5242880, 16384, 128, 1))
    with torch.cuda._DeviceGuard(0):
        torch.cuda.set_device(0)
        buf0 = empty((1, 320, 128, 128), device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)
        # Source Nodes: [out], Original ATen: [aten.gelu, aten.gelu_backward, aten.native_dropout_backward]
        stream0 = get_raw_stream(0)
        triton_poi_fused_gelu_gelu_backward_native_dropout_backward_0.run(tangents_1, gt, primals_1, buf0, 320, 16384, grid=grid(320, 16384), stream=stream0)
        del gt
        del primals_1
        del tangents_1
        return (buf0, )

Here's also a reproducible script for this
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.fx.experimental.proxy_tensor import make_fx
import torch.nn.init as init
from torch import Tensor
from torch.nn.parameter import Parameter

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(
        self,
    ):
        super().__init__()

        self.in_layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Dropout(p=0.1),
        )
        
    def forward(self, x):
        out = F.gelu(x)
        out = self.in_layers(out)

        return out

model = Block()
model = model.to("cuda").to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)

net = torch.compile(model, fullgraph=True)

num_batch = 20
profile_batch = 15

for i in range(num_batch):

    input_t = torch.randn([1, 320, 128, 128], dtype=torch.float32, device='cuda', requires_grad=True)
    input_t = input_t.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)

    target_t = torch.ones_like(input_t)

    if i == profile_batch:
        torch.cuda.cudart().cudaProfilerStart()
    
    out = net(input_t)
    out.backward(target_t)

    if i == profile_batch:
        torch.cuda.cudart().cudaProfilerStop()

Versions

Minified repro
import torch

from typing import List
from torch._dynamo.backends.common import aot_autograd
from functorch.compile import make_boxed_func

torch._dynamo.config.capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops = True #Try dynamic shapes with torch.nonzero...
torch._dynamo.config.capture_scalar_outputs = True #Recommended to set this to True when setting capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops to True

def forward(x):
    batch_size = x.size()[0]
    molecule_size = x.size()[1]
    edges = torch.nonzero(x > 0.5, as_tuple=True)
    index_ij = ((edges[0] * molecule_size * molecule_size) + (edges[1] * molecule_size) + edges[2])
    vx = x.unsqueeze(2).repeat([1,1,8,1])
    vr_dist = torch.linalg.vector_norm((vx.unsqueeze(3) - x.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2)), dim=-1)
    vr_x_ij = torch.abs(vr_dist.transpose(2,3).transpose(1,2).reshape(batch_size*molecule_size*molecule_size, 8).unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1)[index_ij])

    return vr_x_ij

graph_modules = []
def my_compiler(gm: torch.fx.GraphModule, example_inputs: List[torch.Tensor]):
    graph_modules.append(gm)
    return make_boxed_func(gm.forward)

my_compiler = aot_autograd(fw_compiler=my_compiler,bw_compiler=my_compiler)

forward_aot = torch.compile(forward, fullgraph=True, dynamic=True, backend=my_compiler)

device = torch.device("cuda")

x = torch.rand([1, 5, 3], device=device)
x = x.requires_grad_(True)

vr_binned_x_ij = forward_aot(x)

nodes.bodyText:
📚 The doc issue
We need to specify that we could not use torch.compile in official Pytorch runtime docker images.
For CPU images g++ is missing and for GPU flavour it cannot find  libcuda.so.
I don't know if it is the best choice to rely on the devel  image size overhead just to let user compile their models.
/cc @ezyang @msaroufim @wconstab @bdhirsh @anijain2305 @zou3519 @atalman @malfet
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
Advertise this in the documentation or add what it is required to the runtime images to let user compile models

🐛 Describe the bug
torch.export.unflatten unflattens graph to keep the original hierarchy of nn.Module. However, the generated call_module node doesn't contain meta['val'] information that the flattened graph does.
import torch

class InnerModule(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.relu = torch.nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.relu(x)

class TestModule(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.inner_module = InnerModule()

    def forward(self, x, y):
        out = x + y
        out = self.inner_module(out)
        out = out + x
        out = self.inner_module.relu(out)
        return out

exported_program = torch.export.export(
    TestModule(), args=(torch.randn(3), torch.randn(3))
)

for node in exported_program.graph.nodes:
    if node.op != "output":
        try:
            print(node.meta["val"])
        except KeyError:

unflattened_module = torch.export.unflatten(exported_program)

    if node.op != "output":
        try:
            print(node.meta["val"])
        except KeyError:

nodes.bodyText:
We have internal logic in facebook-github-bot that periodically cleaned up stack PR branch when the it is closed, i.e. #116229.  That works fine, but one of the pain point is that the branch is deleted too soon.

If the PR is reverted and the branch has been deleted, it cannot be re-opened to reland.
A stacked PR is owned by the author of the stack, so a deleted branch couldn't be restored by others (to be confirmed)

The potential fix here is to move the logic to OSS bot and increase the amount of waiting time between when the PR is closed and the branch is cleaned up.
cc @ZainRizvi @kit1980 @clee2000 @PaliC @jeanschmidt @malfet
nodes.title: Improve the bot logic that cleans up closed stack PR branch

🐛 Describe the bug
I am trying to measure the runtime of the forward pass of ResNet-50 during training and during evaluation. I am running experiments on a 64-core CPU and no GPU is used. Here is the code I used.
import argparse
import time

import torch
import torch.optim as optim
import torchvision
import torchvision.datasets as datasets
import torchvision.transforms as transforms


parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument(
    "--batch_size",
    type=int,
    default=128,
    help="Batch size.",
)
parser.add_argument("--num_data", default=1024, type=int, help="Number of fake images.")
args = parser.parse_args()


train_dataset = datasets.FakeData(
    args.num_data, (3, 224, 224), 1000, transforms.ToTensor()
)
train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
    train_dataset, batch_size=args.batch_size, num_workers=1, pin_memory=True
)
test_dataset = datasets.FakeData(
    args.num_data, (3, 224, 224), 1000, transforms.ToTensor()
)
test_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
    test_dataset, batch_size=args.batch_size, num_workers=1, pin_memory=True
)

model = torchvision.models.resnet50(pretrained=True)

optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
criterion = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()


print("==================== Training ====================")
model.train()
for i, (images, target) in enumerate(train_loader):
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    start = time.time()
    outputs = model(images)
    end = time.time()
    print(f"Train forward time: {(end - start) * 1000.0} ms")

    loss = criterion(outputs, target)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()


print("==================== Evaluation ====================")
model.eval()
for i, (images, target) in enumerate(test_loader):
    with torch.no_grad():
        start = time.time()
        outputs = model(images)
        end = time.time()
        print(f"Eval forward time: {(end - start) * 1000.0} ms")

I noticed that if I do training first then evaluation, then a forward pass during evaluation is faster than a forward pass during training, which is expected. The runtimes are shown below.

Eval forward time: 1438.7931823730469 ms

However, if I do evaluation only, by commenting out the training code block, then a forward pass during evaluation will be much slower, and even slower than a forward pass during training.
==================== Evaluation ====================
Eval forward time: 2784.9841117858887 ms
Eval forward time: 2838.468551635742 ms

It looks like doing training first could speed up the forward pass during evaluation. How is this possible?

🐛 Describe the bug
Description:
I am encountering an issue while training a Seq2Seq model for English-to-French translation using the Multi30K dataset. The model has been successfully trained on a Windows system with an RTX 3080 GPU, and it also works correctly on a MacBook Pro M3 MAX when using the CPU. However, when I attempt to utilize MPS (Metal Performance Shaders) for faster training on the MacBook Pro, I encounter a problem where the loss value turns into NaN after a few batches in the first epoch.
Steps to Reproduce:

Train the Seq2Seq model on a Windows system with an RTX 3080 GPU (successful training, no issues).
Train the same model on a MacBook Pro M3 MAX using the CPU (successful training, no issues).
Train the model on the MacBook Pro M3 MAX using MPS for faster training.


The training starts normally, processing a few batches successfully.
After a few batches in the first epoch, the loss value turns NaN.

Expected Behavior:
The model should train without the loss value turning into NaN, similar to how it successfully trains on the Windows GPU and the MacBook Pro CPU.
Actual Behavior:
When training with MPS on the MacBook Pro M3 MAX, the loss value becomes NaN after a few batches in the first epoch.

🐛 Describe the bug
Bug Description
Issue: Hang in isend/irecv operations when mixing default and non-default communication groups.
Details: Asynchronous communication operations (isend/irecv) exhibit a hanging issue when alternating between the default communication group and user-defined groups (grp_0 and grp_1). The first set of operations using the default group succeeds, but subsequent operations using grp_0 and grp_1 hang.
Reproduction Steps

Initialize three communication groups:

Default group: Ranks 0-5
grp_0: Ranks 0, 2, 4
grp_1: Ranks 1, 3, 5


Perform isend/irecv operations:

Rank 0 to Rank 2 (default group) - succeeds
Rank 1 to Rank 3 (default group) - succeeds
Rank 0 to Rank 2 (grp_0) - hangs
Rank 1 to Rank 3 (grp_1) - hangs



Expected Behavior
Operations using both default and non-default communication groups should complete successfully without hanging.
Actual Behavior
Operations hang when switching from the default group to grp_0 or grp_1 for the second set of isend/irecv.
Additional Information
This bug only triggers when the world size is larger than four, using the below script.
# Pytorch script
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist

NODE_RANK = int(os.getenv("RANK", '0'))
WORLD_SIZE = int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE"))
MASTER_ADDR = os.environ.get("MASTER_ADDR")
MASTER_PORT = os.environ.get("MASTER_PORT")

class Bug:


    def __init__(self):

        dist.init_process_group(
            backend = "nccl",
            init_method = f"tcp://{MASTER_ADDR}:{MASTER_PORT}",
            rank = NODE_RANK,
            world_size = WORLD_SIZE,
        )

        self.rank = dist.get_rank()
        device_count = torch.cuda.device_count()
        device = self.rank % device_count
        torch.cuda.set_device(device)

        grp_0 = dist.new_group(range(0, WORLD_SIZE, 2), tag=f"grp{self.rank}_0")
        grp_1 = dist.new_group(range(1, WORLD_SIZE, 2), tag=f"grp{self.rank}_1")
        self.grp = grp_0 if self.rank in range(0, WORLD_SIZE, 2) else grp_1


    def run(self):
        
        tensor_recv_shape = torch.empty(
            (3), device=torch.cuda.current_device(), dtype=torch.int64
        )
        tensor_send_shape = torch.ones(
            (3), device=torch.cuda.current_device(), dtype=torch.int64
        )

        tensor_recv = torch.empty(
            (1024), device=torch.cuda.current_device(), dtype=torch.int64
        )
        tensor_send = torch.ones(
            (1024), device=torch.cuda.current_device(), dtype=torch.int64
        )

        if self.rank in [0, 1]:
            op = dist.P2POp(dist.isend, tensor_send_shape, self.rank+2)
            reqs = dist.batch_isend_irecv([op])
            for req in reqs:
                req.wait()
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            print(f"rank {self.rank} isend default group done")
            
            print(f"rank {self.rank} isend non-default group begin")
            op = dist.P2POp(dist.isend, tensor_send, self.rank+2, self.grp)
            reqs = dist.batch_isend_irecv([op])
            for req in reqs:
                req.wait()
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            print(f"rank {self.rank} isend non-default group done")

        else:
            op = dist.P2POp(dist.irecv, tensor_recv_shape, self.rank-2)
            reqs = dist.batch_isend_irecv([op])
            for req in reqs:
                req.wait()
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            print(f"rank {self.rank} irecv default group done")
            
            print(f"rank {self.rank} irecv non-default group begin")
            op = dist.P2POp(dist.irecv, tensor_recv, self.rank-2, self.grp)
            reqs = dist.batch_isend_irecv([op])
            for req in reqs:
                req.wait()
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            print(f"rank {self.rank} irecv non-default group done")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bug = Bug()
    bug.run()

The launch script.
# Launch script
#!/bin/bash

export CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=1
export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=<Your NIC>
export GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=<Your NIC>

export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO
export NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=COLL

export GPUS_PER_NODE=${GPUS_PER_NODE:-2}
export MASTER_ADDR=${MASTER_ADDR:-<Your master address>}
export MASTER_PORT=6000
export NNODES=${NNODES:-3}
export NODE_RANK=${NODE_RANK:-0}
export WORLD_SIZE=$(($GPUS_PER_NODE*$NNODES))

DISTRIBUTED_ARGS="
    --nproc_per_node $GPUS_PER_NODE \
    --nnodes $NNODES \
    --node_rank $NODE_RANK \
    --master_addr $MASTER_ADDR \
    --master_port $MASTER_PORT
"

torchrun $DISTRIBUTED_ARGS test.py

🐛 Describe the bug
Hello,
We've been using FSDP with DTensors and sharded checkpointing. We've noticed that FSDP.optim_state_dict_to_load seems to consume memory proportional to the unsharded model size rather than the sharded size.
The culprit seems to be this slicing operation, which retains the storage of the full tensor in optim_state. Once FSDP.load_state_dict is called these tensors and their storage goes away, but temporarily the memory usage can be much higher than expected.
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/97891b184c12763f335fbe1ff63fab843edafab5/torch/distributed/fsdp/_optim_utils.py#L406C9-L406C9
Our workaround for now has just been to add .clone() at the end of that line.
Versions
We use a slightly patched version of v2.1.1, but the issue still appears to exist on main.

🐛 Describe the bug
My suspicion is that we do not re-enable grad mode for the closure when calling it from within step. Due to this, there is a disparity between eager and dynamo for optimizers with closures that depend on grads getting modified, which...according to #38006, account for all cases where closures are used.
Disclaimer: There is an ongoing issue (#38006) that requires looking into where the example I provide below is potentially abusing the closure (I modify the .grad field of the params within the closure), which the docs say should not happen, but empirical evidence points 100% otherwise. Regardless, we probably want to either ban closures (and error when we notice one) or actually call them correctly.
Error logs
(pytorch-3.10) [janeyx@devgpu023.odn1 ~/local/pytorch (d186986c)]$ python playground2.py 
before compiled loop: param=tensor([[0.6176, 0.6603, 0.8097],
        [0.8297, 0.5115, 0.0299]], device='cuda:0', requires_grad=True)
after compiled loop: param=tensor([[0.6176, 0.6603, 0.8097],
        [0.8297, 0.5115, 0.0299]], device='cuda:0', requires_grad=True)
before eager loop: param_c=tensor([[0.6176, 0.6603, 0.8097],
        [0.8297, 0.5115, 0.0299]], device='cuda:0', requires_grad=True)
after eager loop: param_c=tensor([[0.6166, 0.6593, 0.8087],
        [0.8287, 0.5105, 0.0289]], device='cuda:0', requires_grad=True)

Minified repro
import torch

param = torch.rand(2, 3, dtype=torch.float32, device='cuda', requires_grad=True)
param_c = param.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True)

def closure():
    param.grad = torch.ones_like(param) * 2
    return param.grad

def closure_c():
    param_c.grad = torch.ones_like(param_c) * 2
    return param_c.grad

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([param])
optimizer_c = torch.optim.AdamW([param_c])

def loop(opt, c):
    opt.step(c)

compiled_loop = torch._dynamo.optimize("eager")(loop)

print(f"before compiled loop: {param=}")
compiled_loop(optimizer, closure)
print(f"after compiled loop: {param=}")

print(f"before eager loop: {param_c=}")
loop(optimizer_c, closure_c)
print(f"after eager loop: {param_c=}")

🐛 Describe the bug
While applying the PT2E Quantization flow with x86InductorQuantizer and lowering into Inductor CPP Backend for stable diffusion, we encountered an issue where 15 linear layers failed to be lowered into QLinear and instead used bmm. Upon investigation, we identified that this issue arises when the input of these linear layers has dimensions exceeding 2 and is not contiguous. For instance in model and also this example code.:

In this case, when we do the linear decomposition, it will fallback to bmm as in 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/_decomp/decompositions.py
    
    
        Lines 3965 to 3968
      in
      80c07df
    
  
  
    

        
          
           if vector_rhs: 
        

        
          
               return tensor1_expanded.bmm(tensor2_expanded).squeeze(-1).view(output_shape) 
        

        
          
           else: 
        

        
          
               return tensor1_expanded.bmm(tensor2_expanded).view(output_shape) 
        
    
  


To fix this issue, we may have 2 options:

Ensure the input of linear to be contiguous in somewhere, for example: add input=input.contiguous at 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/_inductor/decomposition.py
    
    
        Lines 460 to 468
      in

               dtype: torch.dtype, 
        

        
          
           ) -> torch.Tensor: 
        

        
          
               return (input.to(torch.float32) - zero_point) * scale 
        
    
  


Add the bmm pattern matcher with extra shape size check inside Inductor and lowering it as qlinear.

                dq_per_channel

🐛 Describe the bug
import itertools
import torch

def fn() -> None:
    a = list(range(1, 3))
    b = list(range(3, 6))
    c = [a, b]
    d = itertools.chain.from_iterable(c)
    return d


comp = torch._dynamo.optimize(nopython=True)(fn)()
While itertools.chain is properly implemented in dynamo, itertools.chain.from_iterable is not. It should be pretty trivial to implement and a good first issue. The only concern is how to properly add it to the itertools dynamo shim as it's a nested class function on the itertools.chain function. We should support this as it's a slightly uncommon way to call arguably the most common itertools utility (itertools.chain).

nodes.title: We don't have an op for aten::view but it isn't a special case.

nodes.bodyText:
This is the root cause of an issue with inductor + dynamic shapes (internal post here with repro).
Normally, inductor tries to match the same output strides as eager, and only attempts to diverge when layout optimization is enabled (when it's determined to be good for perf).
However, it's possible for inductor's outputs to end up with strides different from eager, even if layout optimization is disabled. The divergence appears to be harmless, but it causes issues for dynamic shapes.
Here's a minimal example:
import torch

def f(x):
    tmp = x + 1
    return tmp.view(-1, 1, 2)

x = torch.arange(8, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)
out = f(x)
compiled_out = torch.compile(f)(x)
print(out.shape)  # []
print(compiled_out.shape)
print(out.stride())
print(compiled_out.stride())

# prints:
torch.Size([4, 1, 2])
torch.Size([4, 1, 2])
(2, 2, 1)
(2, 0, 1)

You can see that output.stride()[1] == 2 in eager, but 0 with inductor. That's because it is harmless in this case: The corresponding dim has output.size()[1] == 1, so the stride at this dim is never used in any calculations to compute an offset into the tensor.
Why is this a problem for dynamic shapes
Today, layout optimization and dynamic shapes are known to not play well together, and so their combination is not allowed.
However, it looks like we:
(1) When we have forward outputs that are saved as activations for the backward graph, we detect when inductor gives us different strides from eager for those activations (here)
(2) when this happens, we query inductor for the strides that it's using at runtime, and blat them directly into the backward graph here
(3) Once inductor sees strides that are static shapes, it is free to generate assertions that these shapes are fixed (here)
The net result is that when inductor generates outputs in the forward with different strides from eager (even if harmless), we will end up with static strides in inductor, even if the user made it clear that their strides were dynamic. This results in the spurious stride assertion failure in the link above.
Options for fixes?
I can think of two:
(1) Force inductor not to use stride==0 when it sees that the corresponding dim has size==1
(2) Have our check for "did the strides diverge between inductor and eager" ignore this difference, since we know it is harmless and not the result of doing any layout optimizations.

I'm not sure if categorizing this one as a bug is correct, maybe this is the intended behaviour but if it is please point me to where I can read on why it's done this way.
Code to reproduce:

print(torch.einsum("ikjl", a).shape)

print(torch.einsum("i...l", a).shape)

print(torch.einsum("l...i", a).shape)

Here what I expected was (5, 4, 10, 3) but got (4, 10, 5, 3).

🐛 Describe the bug
envs: cuda11.8 + python3.10 + pytorch2.1 + shark-turbine + iree
model: llama2 from https://github.com/karpathy/llama2.c?tab=readme-ov-file
When I excuted train.py in llama2.c under the right circumstances, first error happened:
NotImplementedError: FIXME: Unsupported placeholder node (this often indicates that a necessary) fx preprocessing pass was not run): {'val': [FakeTensor(..., device='cuda:0', size=(128, 256, 6, 24)), FakeTensor(..., device='cuda:0', size=(128, 256, 6, 24))]}
I figured it out: the 'tensor_meta' in 'meta' of 'unbind' is empty, due to the method 'set_meta' in 'pytorch/torch/fx/experimental/proxy_tensor.py' which writes like:
    if isinstance(val, FakeTensor):
        proxy.node.meta['tensor_meta'] = _extract_tensor_metadata(val)
    elif isinstance(val, torch.Tensor) and not val.is_sparse:
        proxy.node.meta['tensor_meta'] = _extract_tensor_metadata(val)
to solve my problem, i add below:
    if "unbind" in proxy.node.name:
     proxy.node.meta['tensor_meta'] = _extract_tensor_metadata(val[0])
It is not a general solution, watching a fast fix and better support to multiple-outputs nodes.
as for 'unbind' or other nodes who has multiple outs, above method can not handle it, leading the lost of 'tensor_meta'.
Sorry for not checking the newest code, above bug has been fixed. Please keep focus on below issue.
After further research I found that the aten.unbind actually is an op with one output. The output's type is "tuple(tensor)". Oppositely, the 'meta.val' of node 'unbind' looks like [fake_tensorxxx, fake_tensorxxx](list(tensor)). So the conflct happens when I use "torch.compile" with backend "shark-turbine" .
I think this is also a point which need some attention, right?
Another, I can get the graph via shark-turbine, but error occured when excuting
       pm = PassManager.parse("builtin.module(torch-to-iree)")
       pm.run(module.operation)

the error is :
MLIRError: Failure while executing pass pipeline:
error: unknown: 'torch.aten.unbind.int' op requires one result
 note: unknown: see current operation: %108:2 = "torch.aten.unbind.int"(%106, %107) : (!torch.vtensor<[128,256,6,24,2],f32>, !torch.int) -> (!torch.vtensor<[128,256,6,24],f32>, !torch.vtensor<[128,256,6,24],f32>)

I think this is still a compatibility issue: turbine ask for a multi-outputs 'unbind' node before 'getitem', but mlir need a one-output 'unbind' node just like torch. I think it is because this kind of nodes whose output's type is tuple(tensor) haven't been support completely.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
In the following code, conv(x)[:, :, :100] is expected to equal to conv(x[:, :, :100]) as the convolution is point-wise, however, in some cases, it is not. The error is relatively small (0.008 at most) but note that here only one Conv1d layer is used.
import torch
from torch import nn
torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)
torch.manual_seed(0)

conv = nn.Conv1d(96, 96, kernel_size=1).cuda()

x = torch.randn((10, 96, 201)).cuda()
print((conv(x)[:, :, :100] == conv(x[:, :, :100])).all().item())  # False

x = torch.randn((10, 96, 200)).cuda()
print((conv(x)[:, :, :100] == conv(x[:, :, :100])).all().item())  # True

x = torch.randn((1, 96, 201)).cuda()
print((conv(x)[:, :100] == conv(x[:, :100])).all().item())  # True

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Hi! I found out that torch.nn.Conv1d may call different low-level CPU implementations during single script run even if weights, bias and data are the same. It causes slightly different results of calculations and different cputime. This behavior can be reproduced with docker image pytorch/pytorch:2.1.2-cuda11.8-cudnn8-devel and the following code
import os
import torch
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

conv = torch.nn.Conv1d(64,64,1).requires_grad_(False).to('cpu')
data = torch.ones((8, 64, 64)).to('cpu')
print('main thread, pid:', os.getpid())
with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU], record_shapes=True, with_modules=True) as prof:
    fst_out = conv(data)
print(prof.events())

class SimpleDataset(Dataset):

    def __len__(self):
        return 10
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU], record_shapes=True, with_modules=True) as prof:
            mel_features = conv(data)
        print('dataloader thread, pid', os.getpid())
        print(prof.events())
        return mel_features

print('\n--------------------\n')
a = DataLoader(SimpleDataset(), num_workers=1, prefetch_factor=1)
snd_out = next(iter(a))
print('\n-------------\n')
print('diff is:', (fst_out - snd_out).abs().max())

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I am currently engaged in the development of a novel cross-attention mechanism for transformers. In this context, consider the shape of q and k as (b, n, l, d), where b represents the batch number, n denotes the head number, l signifies the sequence length, and d stands for the feature dimensions.
The code mechanism employed to compute attention involves the application of the F.relu activation function to both q and k, followed by reshaping operations. Specifically, it can be expressed as follows:
F.relu(q).reshape(b, n * l, d) @ F.relu(k).reshape(b, n * l, d)
However, the reshape operation results in the multiplication of two large matrices, incurring a substantial GPU memory cost. This presents a notable drawback in terms of computational efficiency and resource utilization.
The aforementioned attention function can be conceptualized as the multiplication between two sparse matrices, considering the involvement of the ReLU function. To address the memory issue, I am seeking to leverage the Batched Sparse Matrix - Batched Sparse Matrix multiplication feature. This enhancement would optimize the computation and alleviate the strain on GPU memory, making the implementation more efficient and scalable.
